Yeah, so power is probably one of the most binding constraints on scaling through the end of the decade. If you look at what a frontier training run might need by 2030, if trends continue, you're talking about something on the order of several gigawatts. That's comparable to a large nuclear plant or more, concentrated in one place. Getting that much power to a single site on that timeline is genuinely hard. You run into grid interconnection queues, transmission buildout, permitting, and local utilities that just aren't set up to hand a few gigawatts to one customer within a couple of years.

Distributing training across multiple data centers helps because you're no longer relying on one location. Instead of finding one site with five gigawatts, you might find several sites with one or two gigawatts each, which is a much more tractable problem. You can tap different parts of the grid, different utilities, places with spare generation or stranded power, and you avoid concentrating all the strain on one region's transmission.

The obvious question is whether you can actually train a single model that way, since training requires a lot of communication between chips. Within a data center you have very high bandwidth interconnects, and between data centers you have much less. But when we looked at it, the bandwidth requirements look manageable. Data parallelism across sites, where each site processes different batches and periodically synchronizes gradients, doesn't need all that much cross-site bandwidth relative to what long-haul fiber can provide, especially if you're willing to lay dedicated fiber, which costs little compared to the cost of the compute itself. There are also algorithmic approaches that reduce how often you need to synchronize, like the low-communication methods people have been developing, which make this even more feasible.

So my sense is that distributed training could substantially relax the power constraint. Rather than being bottlenecked by what a single site can draw, you're bottlenecked more by total power available across a region or a country, which is far larger. It doesn't make the problem disappear, since you still need lots of new generation and energy buildout, but it shifts the constraint from "can we get this much power to one spot" to "can we build enough power overall," and that's a much more forgiving constraint. Combined with growth in chip production, it's part of why I think training runs on the order of 10^29 FLOP or so by 2030 are plausible from a pure feasibility standpoint. Whether companies will actually want to spend the hundreds of billions of dollars that implies is a separate economic question.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So when we looked at the constraints on scaling through 2030 at Epoch, power was the one that stood out as potentially binding earliest, at least if you assume training runs continue to be concentrated in a single campus. If you extrapolate the roughly four- to five-fold annual growth in training compute, you end up with frontier runs in 2030 needing on the order of several gigawatts, maybe up to ten gigawatts or so for a single run. And finding a single site that can deliver that is genuinely hard. You're talking about something comparable to the output of multiple large power plants, and the grid interconnection timelines, the permitting, the transmission upgrades, all of that can take many years.

Geographic distribution changes the shape of that problem quite a lot. Instead of needing one ten-gigawatt site, you can have, say, five or ten campuses each drawing one or two gigawatts, which is already something that's been built or is being built. And then the question becomes whether you can run a single training run across those sites, which is really a networking and algorithms problem rather than a power problem. The bandwidth between data centers is much lower than within one, and the latency is much higher, so you can't just naively extend the usual data-parallel approach. But there's been a fair amount of work on this. Google has been doing multi-datacenter training already, and there are techniques like asynchronous updates, or hierarchical approaches where you do a lot of local communication and only sync across sites occasionally, that can tolerate those constraints. Our rough analysis suggested that with existing fiber infrastructure and plausible improvements, you could connect sites across a region without the communication overhead becoming a huge fraction of the run.

So I think the net effect is that distribution moves power from being perhaps the tightest constraint to something more comparable with the others, like chip production or data availability. It doesn't make power free. You still need to actually build the generation capacity, and in aggregate the US grid is only adding so much per year. But it lets you tap into a lot of existing slack across many locations rather than being bottlenecked on what any one utility can deliver to one spot. My guess is that this ends up being how the largest runs get done later in the decade, essentially by necessity.

astra-6.text:
I think the main benefit is that you don’t have to find all of the power in one place. If you’re trying to build a very large training cluster at a single site, you need a huge amount of electricity available at that location, along with the transmission infrastructure and a grid connection. That can be much harder than finding the same total amount of power spread across several locations.

So, if you can distribute a training run across multiple sites, you can draw on power wherever it’s available. That gives you more flexibility and potentially lets you expand without waiting for one particularly large infrastructure project to finish.

The challenge is communication. During training, chips need to exchange information, and connections between distant data centers have higher latency and typically less bandwidth than connections within a data center. You therefore need to organize the computation so that you’re doing enough useful work between those exchanges to keep the communication overhead manageable.

So I’d think of this as a way to relax the constraint on how much power you need at a single location. It doesn’t eliminate the overall electricity requirement. But through 2030, that flexibility could make a meaningful difference to how quickly training infrastructure can scale.

I think the main benefit is that you no longer need to find all the power for a training run in one place. If you’re trying to build a very large cluster at a single site, you need a huge amount of generation and transmission capacity available at that particular location. That can be much harder than finding the same total amount of power spread across several locations.

So, if we can distribute training across geographically separated data centers, we can tap into multiple regional grids and build wherever power is available. That could make a substantial difference through 2030, because it gives you more flexibility than waiting for one enormous site to get connected.

The catch is communication. Training involves a lot of information moving between chips, and greater distances introduce latency and bandwidth constraints. You’d need to organize the computation so that most of that communication happens locally, with less frequent communication between sites. How much this helps therefore depends on how efficiently we can make those distributed training methods work. It relaxes the requirement to concentrate power in one place, but you still need the electricity overall.
